import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

DOC = "PCR-006"
UO = "viral_inactivation"
UO_TITLE = "Low-pH Viral Inactivation (Step 6)"
# CQAs the step governs: it sets the (cumulative) XMuLV clearance and can increase
# aggregate; acidic charge variants shift negligibly over the hold.
VI_CQAS = ["lrv_xmulv", "aggregates_hmw"]
n_scr = doe_runs(UO, "screening")
n_rsm = doe_runs(UO, "rsm")

agg_fit = D.fit(UO, "rsm", "aggregate_out_pct")

cc = D.center_cv_df(UO, "rsm")

XMULV_STEP = _cc("xmulv_lrf")

VI_MVM = float(vc[vc.step.str.contains("Viral Inactivation")].iloc[0].MVM)
CUM_XMULV = float(V["total_lrv_xmulv"])
xrow = cqa_reg[cqa_reg.key == "lrv_xmulv"].iloc[0]
XMULV_REQ = float(xrow.acc_low)
AGG_LIMIT = cqa_reg[cqa_reg.key == "aggregates_hmw"].iloc[0].acc_high
xmulv_cpk = float(cap[cap.key == "lrv_xmulv"].iloc[0].Cpk)
ph = CFG.unit_op(UO).param("ph")

# Executive summary {.unnumbered}

This report documents the Stage 1 (Process Design) characterization of the A-Mab
low-pH viral inactivation step (Step 6), the dedicated viral-clearance operation in
which the Protein A eluate is held at low pH to inactivate enveloped viruses. The
study was executed under the Process Characterization Plan **PCP-006** on a qualified
scale-down inactivation model, following the lifecycle approach to process validation
[@fda2011], the Quality-by-Design principles of ICH Q8, Q9 and
Q11 [@ichq8; @ichq9; @ichq11], and the viral-safety framework of ICH Q5A
[@ichq5a], with the process model and risk methodology of the A-Mab case study
[@amab2009].

Four process parameters were evaluated. A `{python} n_scr`-run two-level full
factorial screening design identified the significant factors and interactions for
the XMuLV log-reduction, the aggregate and the acidic charge variants; a
`{python} n_rsm`-run face-centred central-composite response-surface design then
quantified main effects, interactions and curvature and defined the multivariate
design space in inactivation pH and hold time.

The low-pH viral inactivation step is demonstrated to be well understood and robust.
The design space, parameter classifications and proven acceptable ranges support the
Stage 2 operating ranges and the viral-safety control strategy, and this report rolls
up into the Process Characterization Master Report (**PCMR-001**).

# Introduction

## Product and unit operation

A-Mab viral safety is assured by a combination of testing and by the demonstrated
capacity of the purification process to clear adventitious and endogenous viruses
[@ichq5a; @amab2009]. Low-pH viral inactivation is the dedicated inactivation step:
the Protein A eluate, already at low pH from the acidic elution, is titrated to the
target inactivation pH, held for a defined time at controlled temperature, and then
neutralized before the next step. Low pH disrupts the lipid envelope of enveloped
viruses and is a robust, well-characterized clearance mechanism for the endogenous
retrovirus-like particles modelled by xenotropic murine leukemia virus (XMuLV); it is
ineffective against non-enveloped viruses such as the parvovirus model MVM, whose
clearance is provided orthogonally by anion exchange and small-virus filtration. This
characterization quantifies how the inactivation parameters govern the XMuLV
log-reduction and the associated product-quality risk of aggregate formation during
the low-pH hold.

## Objectives

The objectives of the study were to (i) establish the quantitative relationships
between the inactivation parameters and the XMuLV log-reduction, the aggregate and the
acidic charge variants; (ii) define the multivariate design space over which the
enveloped-virus inactivation is assured while aggregate remains within its limit;
(iii) establish proven acceptable ranges (PARs) and normal operating ranges (NORs) for
each parameter; (iv) classify each parameter for its risk of impact to CQAs and to
process performance; and (v) provide the process understanding and ranges that justify
the Stage 2 operating conditions and the viral-safety control strategy.

## Regulatory and scientific basis

The work follows the lifecycle approach to process validation of the FDA 2011 guidance
[@fda2011], the FDA 2011 process-validation guidance [@fda2011] and the ICH Q8–Q11
[@fda2011], applies the enhanced (QbD) development approach of ICH Q8, Q9 and Q11
[@ichq8; @ichq9; @ichq11], and addresses viral clearance under ICH Q5A [@ichq5a].
Criticality is treated as a continuum (ICH Q9). The report structure corresponds to
the Stage 1 Process Design Report of the FDA process-validation lifecycle and provides development-report
content suitable to support a Biologics License Application.

# Prior knowledge and quality risk basis

## Platform and prior-product knowledge

Low-pH inactivation is a platform viral-clearance operation whose behaviour is well
established from related humanized IgG1 antibodies and A-Mab experience [@amab2009].
Prior knowledge established that enveloped-virus inactivation increases as the pH is
lowered and as the hold time and temperature increase; that the acceptable pH window is
narrow and high-consequence — above approximately 4.0 the inactivation is incomplete,
while below approximately 3.2 the product is at risk of acid-induced aggregation; and
that aggregate can also form during a prolonged or warm hold. This knowledge framed the
attributes in scope and the prioritization of parameters for characterization.

## Quality attributes in scope

The step sets the (cumulative) enveloped-virus clearance CQA (@tbl-cqa) and carries a
product-quality risk of aggregate formation during the low-pH hold; the acidic charge
variants are followed as they can shift slightly during the hold. Criticality is scored
on the A-Mab continuum using Tool #1 (Risk Score = Impact × Uncertainty); attributes
rated High (H) or Very High (VH) are treated as *Critical* [@amab2009].

```{python}
#| output: asis
show(cqas_for(UO))
```

: Viral-clearance CQA set by the low-pH inactivation step, with acceptance criterion and criticality (Tool #1 = Impact × Uncertainty). {#tbl-cqa}

The XMuLV clearance CQA is expressed as the cumulative log-reduction across the process
(≥ `{python} f"{XMULV_REQ:g}"` log₁₀); this step is the single largest contributor. The
aggregate is a High-criticality size-variant CQA (limit `{python} f"{AGG_LIMIT:g}"`% HMW)
that this step can increase and that the cation-exchange step subsequently polishes.

## Risk-based prioritization and parameter selection

Consistent with the A-Mab lifecycle of iterative risk assessments, the characterization
scope was set by the Pre-Characterization Process Risk Assessment (**RA-001**), which
used prior knowledge and a risk-ranking-and-filtering screen to prioritize parameters
and to assign the study type. Inactivation pH, hold time and temperature, which carry a
credible risk to the enveloped-virus inactivation and to aggregate, were assigned to the
multivariate DoE; A-Mab concentration, expected to affect neither over a wide range, was
assigned to univariate assessment [@amab2009; @fda2011]. The parameters and ranges
carried into this study are given in @tbl-param (§5.1).

# Materials and methods

## Scale-down model and its qualification

All characterization runs were performed on a qualified small-scale inactivation model
operated at the commercial-process equivalents for the acidification, mixing, hold
vessel geometry and temperature control (**SOP-2009**). Viral log-reduction was
determined in spiking studies in which a characterized XMuLV stock was added to the
starting material and the infectious titre measured before and after the hold. The SDM
was qualified against at-scale reference data (**SOP-1001**) by comparing the
operational parameters and the output attributes — XMuLV log-reduction, aggregate and
charge variants — confirming that the model is representative and suitable to support
design-space and PAR claims [@fda2011; @ichq5a]. The between-run reproducibility of the
centre-point condition (§6.1) provides the pure-error term in the lack-of-fit assessment.

## Operation

The Protein A eluate is titrated with acid to the target inactivation pH, mixed, and
held for the defined hold time at controlled temperature; the solution is then
neutralized to the load condition of the next step. Inactivation pH and temperature are
controlled to set-point and the hold time is timed from the attainment of the target pH.
Buffers and the A-Mab concentration of the incoming pool are controlled to platform
specifications and are treated as quality-controlled inputs rather than characterized
variables, except for the concentration range assessed univariately [@amab2009].

## Analytical methods

The step responses were measured by validated methods (@tbl-methods). XMuLV infectious
titre was determined by a TCID50 infectivity assay (**AMV-3017**) and the log-reduction
computed from the pre- and post-hold titres; aggregate by SEC-HPLC (**AMV-3011**); and
acidic charge variants by icIEF (**AMV-3013**). Method performance characteristics are
summarized in Appendix D.

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(sop_table(sops=[], amvs=VIRAL_INACT_AMV_REFS))
```

: Validated analytical methods used in the characterization. {#tbl-methods}

## Sampling plan

Each DoE run was sampled before and after the hold for the XMuLV infectious titre and
sampled at the end of the hold for aggregate and acidic charge variants; in-process pH,
temperature and hold-time records confirmed the run conditions. Centre-point runs were
replicated within each design (three in screening, four in the response-surface design)
to quantify reproducibility and pure error.

## Statistical methods

Designs were constructed and analyzed in coded factors, with each parameter's
characterization range mapped so that the set-point is 0 and the range edges are
±1 (**SOP-1002**). Screening data were analyzed by ordinary-least-squares regression of
each response on the main effects and all two-factor interactions; factor *effects* are
reported as twice the coded coefficient. Response-surface data were analyzed with the
full quadratic model. Statistical significance was assessed at α = 0.05. Model adequacy
was judged by R², the adjusted and predicted R², the overall model F-test, and an
analysis of variance partitioning the residual into lack of fit and pure error; a
non-significant lack-of-fit F-test (p > 0.05) indicates an adequate model. Consistent
with the conservative treatment of viral clearance [@ichq5a], the enveloped-virus
clearance claim is taken from the demonstrated log-reduction rather than from an
extrapolated model. The design space was defined as the region of inactivation pH and
hold time over which the XMuLV log-reduction is assured and aggregate remains within its
limit. Commercial-scale capability of the cumulative XMuLV clearance was estimated by
Monte-Carlo simulation of `{python} f"{V['n_monte_carlo']:,}"` batches with each
parameter varied within its NOR, reporting the one-sided (lower) capability index.

## Screening design

Factor screening used a two-level full factorial in the three multivariate factors
(A–C) with three centre-point replicates, `{python} n_scr` runs in total. The full
factorial estimates all three main effects and all three two-factor interactions without
confounding. The three responses recorded for each run were the XMuLV log-reduction, the
aggregate and the acidic charge variants. The complete coded design matrix and run
responses are given in Appendix A.

## Response-surface design

The three multivariate factors were carried into a face-centred central-composite design
(cube points, axial points at the face centres, and four centre-point replicates),
`{python} n_rsm` runs in total, enabling estimation of curvature in addition to main
effects and interactions. The complete coded design matrix and responses are given in
Appendix B.

## Univariate assessment

A-Mab concentration was evaluated one factor at a time across its characterization range
for its effect on the XMuLV log-reduction and aggregate; it was not carried into the
multivariate design because prior knowledge indicated no credible impact over the range
studied.

pure-error estimate used in the lack-of-fit assessment; the higher coefficient of

Inactivation pH is the dominant factor for the XMuLV log-reduction — the log-reduction
increases as the pH is lowered — followed by hold time and temperature, which also
increase the inactivation. Aggregate, by contrast, is driven principally by hold time and
temperature and is comparatively insensitive to pH over the range studied. The
enveloped-virus inactivation and the aggregate risk therefore respond to a shared set of
factors, which is why a multivariate design space — rather than independent
one-dimensional ranges — is required to assure clearance while limiting aggregate.

## Mechanistic interpretation

The response-surface models reproduce the established behaviour of low-pH inactivation.
Enveloped-virus inactivation is driven primarily by hydrogen-ion concentration: lowering
the inactivation pH accelerates the disruption of the viral lipid envelope and increases
the log-reduction, with additional inactivation from a longer hold and a warmer
temperature. Aggregate formation, in contrast, is a time- and temperature-dependent
process and is comparatively insensitive to pH over the studied window, so the practical
constraint on the hold is the aggregate that accrues at long hold times and high
temperature rather than at low pH. The acceptable pH window is nonetheless narrow and
high-consequence — bounded above by incomplete inactivation and below by the prior-knowledge
risk of acid-induced aggregation — which is why inactivation pH is controlled to a tight
range and treated as the process's only true CPP. Because the mechanism acts on the lipid
envelope, the step provides no clearance of the non-enveloped parvovirus model MVM.

# Design space

The design space is the region of inactivation pH and hold time (at the controlled
temperature) over which the XMuLV log-reduction is assured with margin and the aggregate
remains within its `{python} f"{AGG_LIMIT:g}"`% limit, computed by overlaying the
clearance and aggregate constraints on the fitted models. @fig-vi (right) shows the XMuLV
log-reduction surface with the required per-step floor; the NOR of each parameter
(@tbl-param) — inactivation pH
`{python} f"{ph.nor[0]:g}–{ph.nor[1]:g}"` and hold time
`{python} f"{CFG.unit_op(UO).param('hold_time').nor[0]:g}–{CFG.unit_op(UO).param('hold_time').nor[1]:g}"`
min — lies well inside the region over which clearance is assured, which in turn lies
within the broader knowledge space bounded by the proven acceptable ranges. Movement
within the design space is not a change, whereas movement outside it would require
assessment under the quality system [@amab2009; @ichq8]. Aggregate remains well below its
limit across the entire region, so the binding constraint is the assurance of the
enveloped-virus log-reduction.

# Process capability and robustness

The low-pH inactivation step is the largest single contributor to the enveloped-virus
clearance, providing `{python} f"{VI_XMULV:g}"` log₁₀ of the cumulative
`{python} f"{CUM_XMULV:.1f}"` log₁₀ XMuLV clearance; it provides
`{python} f"{VI_MVM:g}"` log₁₀ of MVM clearance, the non-enveloped parvovirus being
cleared orthogonally by anion exchange and virus filtration. A Monte-Carlo simulation of
`{python} f"{V['n_monte_carlo']:,}"` commercial-scale batches, with every parameter varied
within its NOR, was used to estimate the commercial-scale distributions and process
capability of the CQAs governed by the step (@tbl-cap). Capability is evaluated one-sided
against the lower requirement for viral clearance and the upper limit for aggregate.

```{python}
#| output: asis
show(cap_for(VI_CQAS), floatfmt=".2f")
```

: Commercial-scale process capability for the CQAs governed by the low-pH inactivation step. {#tbl-cap}

The cumulative XMuLV clearance meets its ≥ `{python} f"{XMULV_REQ:g}"` log₁₀ requirement
with a capability of **Cpk = `{python} f"{xmulv_cpk:.2f}"`**. This is the minimum
capability in the drug-substance process and is deliberately conservative: the
viral-clearance requirement is set with a large safety margin, and the demonstrated
clearance exceeds it robustly. Aggregate is held well within its limit with high
capability. The margins confirm that the NOR-bounded step reliably assures viral safety
and product quality at commercial scale.

# Parameter classification

Each parameter was classified on the A-Mab continuum from the demonstrated effects and the
design-space risk (@tbl-class). The rationale is as follows.

- **Inactivation pH — CPP.** pH is the dominant factor for the enveloped-virus
  log-reduction (§6.2–6.3), which is a Very-High-criticality viral-safety CQA (Severity
  ≥ 8), and its acceptable window is narrow and high-consequence in both directions. It is
  therefore a full critical process parameter — the only one in the drug-substance process
  — controlled to a tight NOR with in-process pH verification.
- **Hold time, temperature — WC-CPP.** Each significantly affects both the log-reduction
  and the aggregate, but both are reliably held within the design space by timed,
  temperature-controlled operation, giving a low risk of leaving the space.
- **A-Mab concentration — GPP.** No meaningful impact on the log-reduction or aggregate was
  observed over the wide range studied.

# Contribution to the control strategy

The low-pH viral inactivation step is the primary control point for enveloped-virus
safety: it provides the dominant, robust XMuLV log-reduction and, with the orthogonal
non-enveloped clearance of anion exchange and virus filtration, establishes the total
viral-clearance claim consolidated in **PCMR-001**. Its contribution to the overall
control strategy comprises: control of the CPP (inactivation pH) to a tight NOR with
in-process pH verification; control of the hold time and temperature (WC-CPP) by timed,
temperature-controlled operation; in-process monitoring of pH, temperature and hold time;
and end-of-hold testing of aggregate and charge variants. The aggregate that can form
during the hold is subsequently polished by cation exchange, and the enveloped-virus
clearance is claimed conservatively per ICH Q5A [@ichq5a].

# Discussion

The characterization quantifies the parameter–response relationships for the low-pH
inactivation step, defines a robust multivariate design space, and classifies every
parameter with a data-supported rationale, identifying inactivation pH as the process's
only true CPP. The aggregate model is excellent and predictive; the XMuLV model is
adequate with no significant lack of fit, and its residual variability — inherent to the
infectivity assay — is handled by taking the clearance claim conservatively rather than by
extrapolation, consistent with ICH Q5A. The principal limitation is inherent to
scale-down viral-clearance characterization: absolute log-reduction values are validated in
dedicated spiking studies on the qualified model and confirmed as part of the viral-clearance
validation, and the design space is defined on that model and carried forward with
in-process control. The characterization confirms that inactivation pH requires the most
stringent (CPP) control, whereas hold time and temperature are well-controlled CPPs.

# Conclusions

The A-Mab low-pH viral inactivation step is well understood and robust. The relationships
between the inactivation parameters and the XMuLV log-reduction, aggregate and charge
variants are quantified by DoE; a multivariate design space in inactivation pH and hold
time is established; every parameter range is justified by data; and the cumulative XMuLV
clearance meets its requirement at commercial scale with a capability of Cpk =
`{python} f"{xmulv_cpk:.2f}"`. Inactivation pH is identified as the sole critical process
parameter. The design space, parameter classifications and proven acceptable ranges provide
the basis for the Stage 2 operating ranges and the viral-safety control strategy. This
report rolls up into the Process Characterization Master Report (**PCMR-001**) and provides
the parameter risk basis for the post-characterization process risk assessment.

# Deviations from the plan {.unnumbered}

No deviations from **PCP-006** were recorded. All planned runs were executed and all
planned responses were measured on the qualified scale-down model.
